opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because gradient attributions are kind of the default tool people reach for, and they're cheap, which is a real virtue. But they have this fundamental limitation: a gradient tells you about the local, linear behavior of the network around a single point. It's asking, "if I nudged this parameter or this activation by an infinitesimal amount, how would the output change?" And neural networks are not linear. So you get all the familiar pathologies: saturation, where something is clearly doing a lot of work but the gradient is near zero because you're on a flat part of a nonlinearity, or cases where the gradient is large but actually ablating the thing doesn't matter much.

With stochastic parameter decomposition, we're doing something quite different. We're trying to decompose the parameters themselves into subcomponents, rank-one pieces, and then we learn, for each input, which of those subcomponents are causally necessary. The key word is "causally." The training objective involves actually ablating subcomponents, stochastically, by random amounts, and requiring that the network's output stays the same. So a subcomponent only gets marked as inactive on an input if you can genuinely remove it, to varying degrees, and nothing breaks. That's an interventional notion of importance rather than a first-order approximation of one.

That was actually one of the main motivations for moving from attribution-based parameter decomposition, our earlier method, to SPD. APD leaned on gradient-based attributions to decide which components were active, and we found it was fragile for exactly the reasons I described: the attributions weren't faithful enough, and the method was very sensitive to hyperparameters. Swapping in learned, ablation-tested causal importances made things considerably more robust.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. SPD's importances are more expensive, since you're training a decomposition, and they're only as good as that decomposition. If your subcomponents aren't the right units, then a faithful statement about the wrong units is of limited use. Gradients also have the nice property that you can apply them to any model off the shelf. So I'd see them as complementary in some sense: gradients are a fast, rough heuristic, while SPD aims to give you something closer to a ground-truth statement of which mechanisms the network actually used on a given input. And for the kinds of claims we ultimately want to make in interpretability, especially safety-relevant claims, I think we need that more causal, intervention-grounded notion.

r001.rationale: The response explains that SPD can address gradient saturation generally, but it does not state that its attributions can handle saturated attention.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we spent a fair amount of time on, because when you introduce a new decomposition method, the obvious question is: how do you know the pieces it gives you are actually the pieces the network is using? And one natural sanity check is to compare against gradient attributions, which are the cheap, standard thing everyone already has.

The way I'd frame it is that SPD's attributions and gradient attributions are answering slightly different questions, and the interesting part is where they agree and where they diverge.

Gradient attributions are a first-order approximation. You're asking, "if I perturbed this parameter or this activation a little bit, how much would the output change?" That's a local, linearized story. It's great for a lot of purposes, but it has well-known failure modes — saturation, cases where the function is highly nonlinear in the region you care about, and the fact that it doesn't really tell you about the structure of the computation, just the sensitivity of it.

SPD is doing something more structural. We're decomposing the parameters themselves into components, and then we have what we've been calling causal importance — the question of whether a given component is actually needed to reproduce the network's behavior on a particular input. And the "stochastic" part matters here, because instead of just ablating components and looking at the damage, we're sampling masks over components and training the decomposition so that the network is robust to having unimportant components ablated at random. That means the attributions you get out are closer to a counterfactual, "does this piece matter for this input" notion than a "what's the local slope" notion.

So when we compared them on toy models where we know the ground truth, what we saw is that in the easy regime they line up reasonably well. If there's a clean feature and a clean mechanism that implements it, both methods will point at roughly the same thing. That's reassuring — it means SPD isn't just inventing structure out of nothing.

Where they diverge is more interesting. Gradient attributions tend to be noisier and more distributed. They'll give you a bunch of small nonzero attributions all over the place because, well, almost everything has some nonzero gradient. SPD's attributions are sparser by construction, because we're explicitly optimizing for a decomposition where most components can be ablated on most inputs without consequence. So you get something that looks more like a discrete circuit — this handful of components is on, the rest are off — rather than a heat map.

And then there's the case of things like superposition or compressed computation, where I think gradient attributions genuinely mislead you. If multiple features are sharing the same parameters, the gradient with respect to those parameters doesn't cleanly separate which feature is doing what. SPD is specifically designed to pull those apart into separate components, so the attributions it gives are at the level of mechanisms rather than at the level of raw weights.

Now, I want to be honest about the caveats. SPD is an optimization procedure with its own loss terms and hyperparameters, and the attributions you get depend on how well that optimization went. If the decomposition is bad — if it's split a mechanism across components it shouldn't have, or merged ones it should have kept separate — then the attributions will be bad too, in ways that can be harder to diagnose than a noisy gradient. Gradients are at least unambiguous about what they're computing. So I'd say SPD's attributions are more informative when they're right, but they come with more ways to be wrong.

The other honest caveat is that we're still mostly in toy-model territory for the really careful comparisons. We've done some work on larger models, but the ground truth gets fuzzy fast, and at that point you're comparing two methods neither of which you can fully verify. That's a pretty common situation in interpretability, and I don't think we've escaped it.

So the summary I'd give is: gradient attributions are a good baseline and they're cheap, but they're fundamentally a sensitivity measure. SPD is trying to get at something more like a causal, mechanism-level story, and the attributions reflect that — sparser, more structured, and better at handling the cases where parameters are doing double duty. But the price is that you're trusting an optimization process, and we need better ways of validating it before I'd want anyone to take SPD attributions as ground truth on a frontier model.

r001.rationale: The response says gradients can fail under saturation and claims SPD helps with superposition or compressed computation, but it does not state that SPD attributions can handle saturated attention.

astra-6.text:
I think the main distinction is that gradient attributions tell you about local sensitivity: if you change something a tiny amount, how does the output change? That’s useful, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you what happens when you remove a component entirely. With nonlinearities or saturation, those can be quite different questions.

With stochastic parameter decomposition, we’re trying to decompose the parameters into components whose contributions we can assess by intervening on them. Because the decomposition is trained with components stochastically switched off, it has a more direct connection to those removal experiments.

But I wouldn’t say that automatically makes its attributions correct. Components can interact, and there may not be a unique way to assign credit between them. The important test is whether the attribution predicts what actually happens under an intervention. That’s where I’d want to compare it with gradient methods, rather than just asking which produces a more interpretable-looking explanation.

r001.rationale: The response mentions saturation as a reason gradient sensitivity and component removal can differ, but does not state that stochastic parameter decomposition’s attributions can handle saturated attention.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main distinction is that a gradient tells you about local sensitivity: if I change this parameter or activation a tiny amount, how much does the output change? That’s useful, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you what happens when you remove a component or make a substantial change to it. Nonlinearities and interactions can make those two things quite different.

With stochastic parameter decomposition, we’re trying to find components of the parameters whose contributions we can test through interventions. During training, we stochastically ablate components and ask the decomposition to preserve the model’s behavior using a sparse set of them. So the attribution is more directly connected to what happens when a component is present or absent.

That doesn’t automatically make it a faithful explanation. You still have to check how well the decomposition reproduces the original model, and whether the components behave as expected when you intervene on them. But I’d generally put more weight on an attribution supported by an actual intervention than on a gradient alone.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts gradient sensitivity with intervention-based attribution, but it does not state that stochastic parameter decomposition can handle saturated attention.
